title: 47. Impact of milk production across the lactation curve on cow and calf performance in the Nebraska Sandhills.
content:
Abstract
Selection for increased milk production across the United States has resulted in variable cow and calf productivity responses. This variability may be due to differences in forage quality and the relationship between calf forage and milk intake. The objective of this study was to determine the impact of increasing level of milk production on cow body weight, condition score, reproductive performance, and calf growth in the Nebraska Sandhills. In a 3-yr study, data were collected on 178 mature crossbred cow-calf pairs from March- and May-calving herds. On approximately 30, 60, 90, 120, and 210 d postpartum, individual cow 24-h milk yield was estimated through weigh-suckle-weigh techniques. Woods curve was utilized to determine total milk produced during lactation for each cow. Cow body weight (BW) and body condition score (BCS) were collected 14 d prior to calving, weekly from d 30 through breeding, and at weaning. Calf BW was recorded at each milking. Cow reproductive performance (percent cycling, pregnancy rate, and percent calving in the first 21 d) were not influenced (P > 0.11) by total milk production. In addition, cow BW and BCS were not influenced (P > 0.57 and P > 0.31, respectively) by total milk production. Pre-weaning calf BW was positively associated (P < 0.001) with increased milk production at each weight date. Dam milk yield did not influence (P > 0.65) calf nursing and grazing time at mid- and late-lactation. However, calf feedlot entry BW was not impacted (P = 0.13) by dam’s milk yield. At the end of the feedlot phase, final live BW tended to be impacted (P = 0.09) by the dam’s milk production. At harvest, hot carcass weight tended (P = 0.08) to be associated with the dam’s total milk production. However, steer average daily gain (ADG) in the finishing phase was not (P = 0.67) associated with level of dam milk production. Steer feedlot gain to feed ratio had a tendency to have been impacted (P = 0.09) by dam’s milk yield. Dry matter intake was influenced by (P = 0.02) level the dam’s milk total production. Within the environmental conditions of this study, increased milk production improved pre-weaning calf growth without compromising overall cow–calf production and had limited effects on post-weaning feedlot performance.
